arXiv:2409.18838v2 [gr-qc] 02 Nov 2025

Lipschitz inextendibility of weak null singularities from curvature blow-up

Jan Sbierski ††thanks: School of Mathematics and Maxwell Institute for Mathematical Sciences, University of Edinburgh, James Clerk Maxwell Building, Peter Guthrie Tait Road, Edinburgh, EH9 3FD, United Kingdom; email: Jan.Sbierski@ed.ac.uk
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of weak null singularities without any symmetry assumptions. The proof introduces a new strategy to infer Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility from the blow-up of curvature. The assumed blow-up is expected to be satisfied for weak null singularities in the interior of generic rotating black holes. Thus, we expect the result presented here to directly contribute to the resolution of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in a neighbourhood of subextremal Kerr.

1 Introduction

It is known from the seminal work of Dafermos and Luk [7] that dynamical vacuum black holes, which settle down to a subextremal Kerr black hole in the exterior, also have a Cauchy horizon in the black hole interior to which the Lorentzian metric extends continuously, see Figure 1. Results for the linearised Einstein equations [21], [32], [13] indicate that generically curvature blows up at the Cauchy horizon, turning it into a so-called weak null singularity, terminating the classical time-evolution. This scenario is a special case of the much broader strong cosmic censorship conjecture, according to which the maximal globally hyperbolic development of generic asymptotically flat initial data is inextendible as a suitably regular Lorentzian manifold. The main result of this paper, Theorem 3.14, shows, that the dynamical black hole interiors of [7], supplemented by a curvature blow-up assumption, are locally Lipschitz inextendible across the weak null singularity. The assumed blow-up of curvature is expected to be generically satisfied, see the discussion in Remark 3.17. Thus, we expect the main theorem to provide one of the ingredients for the resolution of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in a neighbourhood of subextremal Kerr initial data.

The result presented in this paper is the first low-regularity (i.e., below Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}) inextendibility result for singular spacetimes which are expected to arise from an open set of initial data. In particular, no symmetry assumptions on the spacetime are made. Existing low-regularity inextendibility results are either restricted to spacetimes with symmetries [30], [8], [31], [33], [18], [22], with warped product structure [31], or are conditional results [8], [5], [11], [28]. An exception are the C0C^{0}-inextendibility results obtained in [9], [23] (see also [10]) which are based on geodesic completeness, do not require any symmetries, and do apply for example to the spacetimes arising from small perturbations of Minkowski initial data [3]. However, these inextendibility results do not concern singularities.

Of the above cited results on singularities the works [30], [8], [33], [18], [22], [5], [11] give C0C^{0}-inextendibility results whereas the work [31] gives a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility result. While for example the works [30], [22], [33], [18] give methods of proof of C0C^{0}-inextendibility which in itself do not rely on any symmetry assumptions, implementing these methods outside of symmetry is challenging for the reason that it is difficult to gain detailed information on, say, light cones or future one-connectedness in spacetimes without any symmetries. Thus, there is a need for either devising new simple ways of gaining such information outside of symmetry or for finding new methods of proof whose implementation is also tractable in spacetimes without any symmetries. This paper contributes to the latter. We will come back to this point after we give a rough outline of the idea of the proof.

First, however, let us think about what it means for a spacetime to be Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible ‘across’ the weak null singularity, i.e, ‘across’ the Cauchy horizon to which the metric extends continuously by [7]: given a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension, we know by [9] that there exists at least one inextendible timelike geodesic in the original spacetime which has a limit point in the extension. Hence, Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of the global spacetime can be shown by establishing that none of the inextendible timelike geodesics in the global spacetime can have a limit point in a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. There are many such inextendible timelike geodesics to consider, see Figure 1: for example τ1\tau_{1} stays in the black hole exterior, while τ2\tau_{2} has a limit point on the Cauchy horizon to which the metric extends continuously by [7]. This exactly gives us the desired notion: a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension across the weak null singularity is a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension in which a timelike geodesic τ2\tau_{2}, which has a limit point in the continuous extension of [7], also has a limit point.

We now give the rough outline of the proof, which is by contradiction. Assume that a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension across the weak null singularity exists. In the first step we go over from the arbitrary timelike geodesic, which has a limit point in the C0C^{0}-extension of [7] as well as in the assumed Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension, to a well-chosen null geodesic which approaches the same limit points in the respective extensions. This step relies on a result from the precursor [34] to this paper.

In the second step we embed this particular null geodesic into a space-filling congruence of null geodesics and use upper bounds on the connection coefficients (in the gauge used in [7]) to show that the C1C^{1}-structure of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension has to be locally equivalent to the C1C^{1}-structure of the C0C^{0}-extension constructed in [7]. Indeed, this local uniqueness problem for Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions was studied in [34] and here, we verify that the assumptions of [34] are met so that we can conclude the local equivalence of C1C^{1}-structures. An important consequence is that a vector field which extends continuously in the C0C^{0}-extension of [7], also extends continuously in the assumed Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension.

In the third step we use the assumed blow-up of curvature: contract curvature with four vector fields which extend continuously in the C0C^{0}-extension of [7] and integrate over a sequence of compact regions asymptotically touching the weak null singularity. We assume that this sequence of integrals diverges. On the other hand, using the coordinates of the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension, in which the Christoffel symbols remain uniformly bounded, we rewrite these integrals over curvature in terms of these Christoffel symbols. By virtue of the equivalence of the C1C^{1}-structures, the vector fields in this integral are also regular with respect to those coordinates.11 1 Indeed, we need that these vector fields are C1C^{1}, but the equivalence of the C1C^{1}-structures only gives that the vector fields are continuous. This is the reason for an additional smoothing procedure, which, as a consequence, requires that the integrals over curvature also diverge if we insert vector fields which are ε\varepsilon-close to the original ones. One can now use Stokes’ theorem to convert the integral over first derivatives of Christoffel symboles, which appears in curvature, into a boundary integral over Christoffel symbols. The expression obtained is then manifestly finite and uniformly bounded along the sequence, thus giving the desired contradiction.

The proof given here establishes for the first time an implication that curvature blow-up leads to low-regularity inextendibility.22 2 For the reverse direction, namely to prove extendibility under curvature bounds, we refer the reader to [27] and references therein. For synthetic curvature blow-up in extensions, see [12]. The subtleties of such a connection were demonstrated in [25]. On the other hand, the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of spherically symmetric weak null singularities was shown in [31] using a method based on direct computation of holonomy. While this method is in principle also applicable to weak null singularities without symmetry assumptions as considered in this paper, it would require, in addition to the control of the C1C^{1}-structure, (pointwise) blow-up bounds on one of the connection coefficients (namely χ\chi, see Section 2.2). The new approach presented here is more parsimonious in the sense that only an integrated blow-up bound on curvature is needed, which is easier to establish analytically.

The Lipschitz inextendibility proven in this paper is an important and critical threshold-regularity: firstly, it captures geometrically that the Levi-Civita connection blows up, which is the geometric object at regularity between the metric and curvature. Secondly, Lorentzian causality below Lipschitz regularity changes drastically in comparison to the familiar one of smooth metrics [4]. Nevertheless, the problem of how to capture geometrically the ‘rate of the blow up’ of the connection, i.e., an inextendibility statement in C0∩Wloc1,pC^{0}\cap W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}, 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, remains a challenging open problem (but see Remark 3.38 for a possible generalisation of the approach presented in this paper).

1.1 Preliminaries

All manifolds considered in this paper are assumed to be smooth. We begin now by recalling two fundamental definitions and the result which constitutes the starting point for most low-regularity inextendibility results.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Lorentzian manifold and let Γ\Gamma be a regularity class, for example Γ=Ck\Gamma=C^{k} with k∈ℕ∪{∞}k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} or Γ=Cloc0,1\Gamma=C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}. A Γ\Gamma-extension of (M,g)(M,g) consists of a smooth isometric embedding ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} of MM into a Lorentzian manifold (M~,g~)(\tilde{M},\tilde{g}) of the same dimension as MM where g~\tilde{g} is Γ\Gamma-regular and such that ∂ι⁡(M)⊆M~\partial\iota(M)\subseteq\tilde{M} is non-empty.

Note that for a Γ\Gamma-extension of (M,g)(M,g) to exist the metric gg has to be at least Γ\Gamma-regular.

2 The spacetimes considered and gauge choice

2.1.1 Localisation: relation to [7]

The double null gauge used here is the one used in [7]. However, in [7] a semi-global region of the black hole interior is constructed, see the shaded region in Figure 2. This shaded region corresponds to the manifold 𝒲×𝕊2\mathcal{W}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} with (u,u¯,θA)(u,\underline{u},\theta^{A}) coordinates, where 𝒲={(u,u¯)∈(−∞,uf)×(−∞,0)|u−12​κ​log⁡(−2​κ​u¯)≥CR}\mathcal{W}=\{(u,\underline{u})\in(-\infty,u_{f})\times(-\infty,0)\;|\;u-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\log(-2\kappa\underline{u})\geq C_{R}\}, where uf≤−1u_{f}\leq-1, CR∈ℝC_{R}\in\mathbb{R}, κ>0\kappa>0 are constants. The metric in these coordinates takes the form (2.1) and with respect to the (u,u¯,θA)(u,\underline{u},\theta^{A}) differentiable structure extends continuously to {u¯=0}\{\underline{u}=0\}, i.e., to 𝒲¯×𝕊2\overline{\mathcal{W}}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}, where 𝒲¯={(u,u¯)∈(−∞,uf)×(−∞,0]|u−12​κlog(−2κu¯)≥CR}\overline{\mathcal{W}}=\{(u,\underline{u})\in(-\infty,u_{f})\times(-\infty,0]\;|\;u-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\log(-2\kappa\underline{u})\geq C_{R}\}. The so attached boundary ∂(𝒲¯×𝕊2)\partial(\overline{\mathcal{W}}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}) at {u¯=0}\{\underline{u}=0\} is called the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. Note that it is a null hypersurface, since u¯\underline{u} is a null coordinate. It is for u¯↗0\underline{u}\nearrow 0 that we expect curvature to blow up. Once this is established, we would call 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} a weak null singularity.

Consider now a timelike geodesic τ2\tau_{2} with a limit point on 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. As discussed in the introduction, in order to show that there are no Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extensions across 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, we need to show that τ2\tau_{2} cannot also have a limit point in a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. But this is a local problem to study: we may now take a small (u,u¯)(u,\underline{u})-chunk of 𝒲×𝕊2\mathcal{W}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} which contains the future end of τ2\tau_{2} close to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} and rescale the (u,u¯)(u,\underline{u})-coordinates by a finite constant factor to bring it into the form of (M,g)(M,g) considered above. Now, since (M,g)(M,g) isometrically embeds into the semi-global spacetime 𝒲×𝕊2\mathcal{W}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}, any Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension of 𝒲×𝕊2\mathcal{W}\times\mathbb{S}^{2} in which τ2\tau_{2} has a future limit point would also give rise to a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension of MM in which τ2\tau_{2} has a future limit point. So if we show that no such extension exists for MM, then the same holds for 𝒲×𝕊2\mathcal{W}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}.

This shows that for our purpose it is sufficient to only consider a finite chunk (M,g)(M,g) of the interior of the dynamical black hole constructed in [7]. Each of those finite chunks (M,g)(M,g) of the weak null singularity is expected to satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 3.14.

2.1.2 About the concept of a weak null singularity

Above, we have described an example which we refer to as a weak null singularity. One may attempt to define the notion of a weak null singularity independently of particular examples. One such attempt is as follows: given a (globally hyperbolic) Lorentzian manifold (M,g)(M,g), a weak null singularity is present if (M,g)(M,g) admits a C0C^{0}-extension ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M} such that part of the boundary of MM in M~\tilde{M} is given by a smooth null hypersurface 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Furthermore, (M,g)(M,g) is Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible across 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

The notion of being Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible ‘across’ 𝒩\mathcal{N} is as explained in the introduction: no Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension exists which provides limit points for timelike geodesics which also have limit points on 𝒩\mathcal{N} in M~\tilde{M}.

In this case on may choose to identify 𝒩\mathcal{N} with the weak null singularity. Note that this is in general dependent on the particular choice of C0C^{0}-extension ι:M↪M~\iota:M\hookrightarrow\tilde{M}, cf. [2].

According to this definition, weak null singularities may come in different strengths. Some may be only Cloc1,1C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible across 𝒩\mathcal{N}, some may be Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendible and some may be even more singular. Based on the expected singular behaviour of the metric near the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} in particular coordinates, we would expect that the weak null singularities in the interior of dynamical black holes are even inextendible in C0∩Wloc1,pC^{0}\cap W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}} for p>1p>1.

See already the left hand side of Figure 4 on page 4 for an illustration of the set-up of Theorem 3.14. Let us remark that the theorem only requires bounds on a subset of the connection coefficients. Bounding a connection strongly relies on the chosen frame – here we use the frame introduced in Section 2.2. We also briefly comment on the structure of the assumptions in the theorem: assuming the existence of a Lipschitz extension through a point p¯∈∂M¯\overline{p}\in\partial\overline{M} in the sense that a timelike geodesic leaves through this point, the first neighbourhood W¯⊆M¯\overline{W}\subseteq\overline{M} arises just as a neighbourhood of p¯\overline{p} which must also be contained in the extension. And while curvature may be bounded in the direction of isolated points on ∂M¯∩W¯\partial\overline{M}\cap\overline{W}, the next statement is that one can always find an open set of boundary points towards which curvature blows up.

Remark 3.17 (Discussion of the assumptions).

All of the assumptions made in the setting of Proposition 3.6 are satisfied for each such finite chunk (M,g)(M,g) of the Cauchy horizon by the work [7] of Dafermos and Luk. The bound (3.15) is not contained as a formal statement in [7] and requires some more work to establish. Note, however, that for weak null singularities only the geometry transversal to the weak null singularity becomes singular – the tangential geometry remains regular, cf. [19, Theorem 3]. For the vector fields X¯i\overline{X}_{i} the expectation is that the choice X¯1=X¯3=e4\overline{X}_{1}=\overline{X}_{3}=e_{4} and X¯2=eA\overline{X}_{2}=e_{A}, X¯4=eB\overline{X}_{4}=e_{B} gives (3.16). Indeed, unpublished work1010 10 It may appear as part of forthcoming work. by the author shows that the result of [32] can be slightly improved so that the version of (3.16) for the linear Teukolsky field (linearised curvature) is satisfied. Alternatively, this follows from the recent work [13].

Remark 3.18 (Slight variation of Theorem 3.14).

Note that for spacetimes satisfying the vacuum Einstein equations (3.16) reduces to a condition on the Weyl curvature tensor. Thus, in this case, R⁡(e4,eA,e4,eB)R(e_{4},e_{A},e_{4},e_{B}) is symmetric in AA and BB and trace-free with respect to γ\gamma – it thus has two independent components. We have the following slight variation of Theorem 3.14 which allows for a combined consideration of these two independent components. The statements are identical up to the following modification:

…and which, moreover, satisfies the following property: there exist continuous vector fields X¯i(j)\overline{X}_{i}^{(j)} on V¯\overline{V}, i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4, j=1,2j=1,2, and an ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such that for any continuous vector fields X^i(j)\hat{X}_{i}^{(j)} on V¯\overline{V} with supV¯‖X^i(j)−X¯i(j)‖h<ε0\sup_{\overline{V}}||\hat{X}_{i}^{(j)}-\overline{X}_{i}^{(j)}||_{h}<\varepsilon_{0} we have

(3.19) |∫V¯∩{u¯<u¯k}R(X^1(1),X^2(1),X^3(1),X^4(1))+iR(X^1(2),X^2(2),X^3(2),X^4(2))vol|→∞\Big|\int\limits_{\overline{V}\cap\{\underline{u}<\underline{u}_{k}\}}R(\hat{X}_{1}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{2}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{3}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{4}^{(1)})+\mathrm{i}R(\hat{X}_{1}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{2}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{3}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{4}^{(2)})\,\mathrm{vol}\Big|\to\infty

along a sequence u¯k→0\underline{u}_{k}\to 0.

Here, i\mathrm{i} is the complex unit.1111 11 One may have also written (3.37) as the norm of a vector in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Setting X¯i(j)=e4\overline{X}_{i}^{(j)}=e_{4} for i=1,3i=1,3, j=1,2j=1,2, X¯2(j)=e1\overline{X}_{2}^{(j)}=e_{1} for j=1,2j=1,2, X¯4(1)=e1\overline{X}_{4}^{(1)}=e_{1}, and X¯4(2)=e2\overline{X}_{4}^{(2)}=e_{2} now combines both components. We expect to apply the theorem in this form in the non-linear setting. The proof of the variation represents only a minor modification of the proof of Theorem 3.14 and will be addressed below.

Remark 3.20 (Relation to global inextendibility result).

The above theorem serves as one piece in a global low-regularity inextendibility statement of generic rotating vacuum black hole spacetimes. Such statements are proven by contradiction. Assuming the existence of a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension, one knows that there is an inextendible timelike geodesic in the original spacetime that has a limit point in the extension (Theorem 2 in [9], Theorem 3.2 in [29], see also [23]). One then leads this statement to a contradiction by showing that none of the inextendible timelike geodesics can leave into a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. Here, one has to take the different geometries along those geodesics into account. Theorem 3.14 deals with those timelike geodesics approaching the weak null singularity, e.g. τ2\tau_{2} in Figure 1. For timelike geodesics lying outside the black hole, for example τ1\tau_{1} in Figure 1, one uses their completeness to derive a contradiction [9]. The geometry in the interior of the black hole to the future of the weak null singularity is still not well-understood, but see for example [1], [37], [38] for scenarios involving and evidence for additional spacelike singularities.

Remark 3.21 (Structure of condition (3.16)).

The structure of the blow-up condition (3.16) is sharp in the following two senses: one can neither bring the absolute value inside the integral nor can one require (3.16) solely for the particular choice X¯i\overline{X}_{i} of vector fields. Counterexamples to both formulations are presented in Examples 4.7 and 4.8 in Section 4.

The statement of the theorem is adapted to the double null gauge chosen in [7], since presently this is the main application of this result. However, note that a double null gauge as in [19] would slightly change the statement of Theorem 3.14; in particular no assumption of the form (3.15) would be needed.

In the fifth step we use Stokes theorem for manifolds with corners and bound again the first order terms as before. In the sixth step we bound again the first order terms as before, estimate the integral of the three-form over the boundary by the corresponding density, and also split the boundary integral into a kk-dependent part and estimate the remaining part by the integral over all of ∂id⁡(V¯)\partial\mathrm{id}(\overline{V}). Finally, the last integral is an integral of a continuous 33-density over a compact piecewise C1C^{1} boundary and thus finite, while to see the uniform boundedness of the first integral we may pull it back via id\mathrm{id} to obtain

∫V¯∩{u¯=u¯k}|X^i⌟vol~|=∫V¯∩{u¯=u¯k}−det​g~|X^iu¯|dudθ1dθ2.\int\limits_{\overline{V}\cap\{\underline{u}=\underline{u}_{k}\}}|\hat{X}_{i}\lrcorner\tilde{\mathrm{vol}}|=\int\limits_{\overline{V}\cap\{\underline{u}=\underline{u}_{k}\}}\sqrt{-\mathrm{det}\tilde{g}}|\hat{X}_{i}^{\underline{u}}|\,dud\theta^{1}d\theta^{2}\;.

Since the integrand and the domain of integration are uniformly bounded in kk, this integral is also uniformly bounded. This gives the contradiction to (3.35) and thus concludes the proof of the main theorem. ∎

Proof of Remark 3.18.

Step 1 and Step 2 are identical. In Step 3, the only modification is that instead of only extending and then smoothing out the four vector fields X¯i\overline{X}_{i} we extend and smooth out the eight vector fields X¯i(j)\overline{X}_{i}^{(j)} to obtain in place of (3.34)

supV¯‖X^i(j)−X¯i(j)‖h<ε0.\sup_{\overline{V}}||\hat{X}_{i}^{(j)}-\overline{X}_{i}^{(j)}||_{h}<\varepsilon_{0}\;.

Then, along a sequence u¯k→0\underline{u}_{k}\to 0 we have by assumption (3.37)

|∫V¯∩{u¯<u¯k}R(X^1(1),X^2(1),X^3(1),X^4(1))+iR(X^1(2),X^2(2),X^3(2),X^4(2))vol|→∞.\Big|\int\limits_{\overline{V}\cap\{\underline{u}<\underline{u}_{k}\}}R(\hat{X}_{1}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{2}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{3}^{(1)},\hat{X}_{4}^{(1)})+\mathrm{i}R(\hat{X}_{1}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{2}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{3}^{(2)},\hat{X}_{4}^{(2)})\,\mathrm{vol}\Big|\to\infty\;.

But this implies that, possibly along a subsequence, we must have

for j=1j=1 or j=2j=2. This now again puts us into the setting of (3.35) and the remainder of the proof proceeds as before. ∎

Remark 3.38.

The method introduced in Step 3 of the proof also gives a possible approach for obtaining an inextendibility statement with g~∈C0\tilde{g}\in C^{0} and ∂g~∈Lloc2\partial\tilde{g}\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}: if the extension is assumed to only have this regularity, then the boundary term in (3.36) is not necessarily bounded. With a minor modification, taking care of the boundary terms in the angular and the uu direction, one can now square the whole estimate up to this point and integrate again in u¯k\underline{u}_{k} to get an expression which has to be finite for g~\tilde{g} in the above regularity class. If on the other hand the corresponding doubly integrated (and squared) curvature expression is assumed infinite, one again obtains the desired contradiction. The main problem with implementing this idea of proof is that the analogue of Step 2 is not known to hold; below Lipschitz regularity the methods of [34] break down. Indeed, in [2] it is shown that weak null singularities as considered here admit continuous extensions for which the identification map id\mathrm{id} does not extend as a C1C^{1}-regular diffeomorphism to the boundary!

4 Examples and counterexamples

As discussed in the introduction, the main application of Theorem 3.14 is to the Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility of weak null singularities occurring in the interior of perturbations of rotating black holes. Since the Kerr family of black holes is expected to comprise all stationary asymptotically flat vacuum black holes, such weak null singularities are expected to occur in the interior of any generic asymptotically flat vacuum black hole. The gauge, with respect to which Theorem 3.14 is formulated, is that of [7] – so that the inextendibility theorem is directly applicable in this context once the integrated curvature blow-up condition (3.16) (and (3.15)) is established. Other (prospective) applications are to weak null singularities without symmetries for the Einstein-Euler equations [35], spherically symmetric weak null singularities for the Einstein-Maxwell-(charged) scalar field/null dust system (see discussion below Example 4.5), and Milne-like spacetimes for a specific range of scale factor, cf. [17, Theorem 3.4].

In this section we give an explicit simple toy-example in spherical symmetry to which Theorem 3.14 is applicable.1818 18 Recall that the advantage of the method presented in this paper is that it is easy to handle even in spacetimes that do not have any symmetry. So the main purpose of the spherically symmetric examples presented in this section is to illustrate the new method in itself in its simplest setting. A modification of this toy-example also shows that the condition (3.16) on curvature blow-up is optimal in the sense that one can neither bring the absolute value inside the integral nor can one demand (3.16) for the X¯i\overline{X}_{i} only instead of the perturbed vector fields X~i\tilde{X}_{i} – both cases are compatible with the existence of a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension. This proves Remark 3.21.

Of course, the spacetime in Example 4.5 does not arise from the Einstein equations coupled to a suitable matter model in a physically interesting situation. However, slightly more complicated spherically symmetric weak null singularities – with Ω⁡(u,u¯)\Omega(u,\underline{u}) and r⁡(u,u¯)r(u,\underline{u}) – do arise in the study of the spherically symmetric Einstein equations coupled to suitable matter models, see for example [15], [26], [24], [6], [20], [36]. We refrain from computing here the curvature tensors and from showing how Theorem 3.14 applies in those settings, since a satisfactory Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-inextendibility criterion tailored to those situations, with input only at the level of first derivatives of the metric, has already been presented in [31].

We now continue to use Example 4.1 to discuss in which sense condition (3.16) is sharp. We start by showing that bringing the absolute value in (3.16) inside of the integral is compatible with the existence of a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension.

Example 4.7.

In the setting of Example 4.1 we define ∂u¯2r⁡(u¯):=1u¯​sin⁡(1u¯)\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r(\underline{u}):=\frac{1}{\underline{u}}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}}) and fix ∂u¯r⁡(u¯):=∫−1u¯1u¯′​sin⁡(1u¯′)​d​u¯′\partial_{\underline{u}}r(\underline{u}):=\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}. We claim that ∂u¯r⁡(u¯)\partial_{\underline{u}}r(\underline{u}) is uniformly bounded in absolute value. To see this we use the substitution x=−1u¯x=-\frac{1}{\underline{u}} to obtain

∫−1u¯1u¯′​sin⁡(1u¯′)​d​u¯′=∫1x⁡(u¯)1x′sin(x′)dx′=−∫1x⁡(u¯)1x′dd​x′cos(x′)dx′=−1x⁡(u¯)​cos⁡(x⁡(u¯))+1​cos⁡(1)−∫1x⁡(u¯)1(x′)2​cos⁡(x′)​d​x′.\begin{split}\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}&=\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}\frac{1}{x^{\prime}}\sin(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}=-\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}\frac{1}{x^{\prime}}\frac{d}{dx^{\prime}}\cos(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}\\ &=-\frac{1}{x(\underline{u})}\cos(x(\underline{u}))+1\cos(1)-\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}\frac{1}{(x^{\prime})^{2}}\cos(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}\;.\end{split}

From this we obtain the crude bound |∂u¯r|≤4|\partial_{\underline{u}}r|\leq 4. We now define r⁡(u¯)=5+∫−1u¯∂u¯r⁡(u¯′)​d​u¯′r(\underline{u})=5+\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}\partial_{\underline{u}}r(\underline{u}^{\prime})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}, which extends continuously to u¯=0\underline{u}=0. Clearly, we have r≥1r\geq 1. In the (u,u¯,θ,φ)(u,\underline{u},\theta,\varphi)-differentiable structure we can now even construct a Lipschitz extension of (M,g)(M,g) across {u¯=0}\{\underline{u}=0\} by simply setting r⁡(u¯)=r⁡(0)r(\underline{u})=r(0) for u¯>0\underline{u}>0.

On the other hand, using the vector fields X¯1=X¯4=∂u¯\overline{X}_{1}=\overline{X}_{4}=\partial_{\underline{u}} and X¯2=X¯3=∂θ\overline{X}_{2}=\overline{X}_{3}=\partial_{\theta} we obtain as in (4.6)

|R⁡(X^1,X^2,X^3,X^4)|≥|r​∂u¯2r|⋅|1+𝒪⁡(ε0)|−𝒪⁡(ε0).|R(\hat{X}_{1},\hat{X}_{2},\hat{X}_{3},\hat{X}_{4})|\geq|r\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r|\cdot|1+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon_{0})|-\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon_{0})\;.

Choose now ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such that 1+𝒪⁡(ε0)≥121+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon_{0})\geq\frac{1}{2}. Also use r≥1r\geq 1 and note that

∫−1u¯|∂u¯2r|(u¯′)​d​u¯′=∫−1u¯|1u¯′​sin⁡(1u¯′)|​d​u¯′=∫1x⁡(u¯)|1x′​sin⁡(x′)|​d​x′\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}|\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r|(\underline{u}^{\prime})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}=\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}|\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})|\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}=\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}|\frac{1}{x^{\prime}}\sin(x^{\prime})|\,dx^{\prime}

is divergent.

The next example shows that it is essential to have the blow up (3.16) not just for the vector fields X¯i\overline{X}_{i}, but indeed also for vector fields X^i\hat{X}_{i} which are C0C^{0}-close to the X¯i\overline{X}_{i} with respect to the metric hh.

Example 4.8.

Again, we consider the setting of Example 4.1 and define r⁡(u¯):=2−∫−1u¯cos⁡(−1u¯′)​d​u¯′r(\underline{u}):=2-\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}\cos(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}. Thus, we have r≥1r\geq 1 and r⁡(u¯)r(\underline{u}) extends continuously to u¯=0\underline{u}=0. Moreover, we have ∂u¯r=−cos⁡(−1u¯)\partial_{\underline{u}}r=-\cos(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}}) and hence we can construct again a Cloc0,1C^{0,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}-extension across {u¯=0}\{\underline{u}=0\} by setting r⁡(u¯)=r⁡(0)r(\underline{u})=r(0) for u¯>0\underline{u}>0.

Now, we compute ∂u¯2r⁡(u¯)=1u¯2​sin⁡(−1u¯)\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r(\underline{u})=\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{2}}\sin(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}}) and we consider the vector fields X¯2=X¯3=1r∂θ\overline{X}_{2}=\overline{X}_{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}\partial_{\theta} and X¯1=X¯4=1−u¯​sin⁡(1u¯)∂u¯\overline{X}_{1}=\overline{X}_{4}=\sqrt{1-\underline{u}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}})}\partial_{\underline{u}}, which are continuous on M¯\overline{M}. Recalling Ru¯​θ​θ​u¯=r​∂u¯2rR_{\underline{u}\theta\theta\underline{u}}=r\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r, we have

(4.9) R⁡(X¯1,X¯2,X¯3,X¯4)=∂u¯2r⁡(u¯)⋅(1−u¯​sin⁡(1u¯))=sin⁡(−1u¯)​(1−u¯​sin⁡(1u¯))​1u¯2.R(\overline{X}_{1},\overline{X}_{2},\overline{X}_{3},\overline{X}_{4})=\partial_{\underline{u}}^{2}r(\underline{u})\cdot\big(1-\underline{u}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}})\big)=\sin(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}})\big(1-\underline{u}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}})\big)\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{2}}\;.

Using again the substitution x=−1u¯x=-\frac{1}{\underline{u}}, we note that the integral of (4.9) in u¯\underline{u} is unbounded:

∫−1u¯sin⁡(−1u¯′)​(1−u¯′​sin⁡(1u¯′)CLOSEOPEN)​1(u¯′)2​d​u¯′=∫1x⁡(u¯)sin⁡(x′)​(1−1x′​sin⁡(x′)​d​x′CLOSE=−cos(x(u¯))+cos(1)−∫1x⁡(u¯)1x′sin2(x′)dx′→−∞for u¯→0.\begin{split}\int_{-1}^{\underline{u}}\sin(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})\big(1-\underline{u}^{\prime}\sin(\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})&\big)\frac{1}{(\underline{u}^{\prime})^{2}}\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}=\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}\sin(x^{\prime})\big(1-\frac{1}{x^{\prime}}\sin(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}\\ &=-\cos(x(\underline{u}))+\cos(1)-\int_{1}^{x(\underline{u})}\frac{1}{x^{\prime}}\sin^{2}(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}\to-\infty\qquad\textnormal{for }\underline{u}\to 0\;.\end{split}

This entails that condition (3.16) is satisfied for the particular choice of vector fields X¯i\overline{X}_{i}, i=1,2,3,4i=1,2,3,4, despite the existence of a Lipschitz extension.

Note, however, that this divergence is unstable under arbitrarily small C0C^{0}-perturbations of the vector fields X¯i\overline{X}_{i}: consider the continuous vector fields X^1=X^4=∂u¯\hat{X}_{1}=\hat{X}_{4}=\partial_{\underline{u}} and X^2=X^3=X¯2=X¯3\hat{X}_{2}=\hat{X}_{3}=\overline{X}_{2}=\overline{X}_{3}. Note that we have ‖X^1−X¯1‖h→0||\hat{X}_{1}-\overline{X}_{1}||_{h}\to 0 for u¯→0\underline{u}\to 0 and thus, by suitably modifying these vector fields for u¯≤−δ\underline{u}\leq-\delta, where δ>0\delta>0, the perturbed vector fields can be arranged to be arbitrarily close to the unperturbed ones. Moreover, we have

∫−δu¯R⁡(X^1,X^2,X^3,X^4)​d​u¯′=∫−δu¯sin⁡(−1u¯′)​1(u¯′)2​d​u¯′=∫1δx⁡(u¯)sin⁡(x′)​d​x′=−cos⁡(x⁡(u¯))+cos⁡(1δ),\int_{-\delta}^{\underline{u}}R(\hat{X}_{1},\hat{X}_{2},\hat{X}_{3},\hat{X}_{4})\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}=\int_{-\delta}^{\underline{u}}\sin(-\frac{1}{\underline{u}^{\prime}})\frac{1}{(\underline{u}^{\prime})^{2}}\,d\underline{u}^{\prime}=\int_{\frac{1}{\delta}}^{x(\underline{u})}\sin(x^{\prime})\,dx^{\prime}=-\cos(x(\underline{u}))+\cos(\frac{1}{\delta})\;,

which is uniformly bounded.
